title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
hook: the Samkhya Karika begins the way a doctor does: there is pain, and the remedies on hand don't finish the job

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika closed with adrishta, the unseen left behind by what we do. A third school opens today.

A headache, again. You take something for it, and it works, for a while. Then it's back next week. A bad night of worry: you call a friend, it helps, and two nights later it's back. A storm takes out the power and there's nothing to do but wait. Some pain comes from inside us, some from other people, some from the weather and the world. The fixes in the drawer are real, but they don't finish the job. Today's school opens right there, the way a good doctor would, by asking what actually ends it.
screen: `THE HEADACHE COMES BACK.` → `THE FIXES IN THE DRAWER.` → `WHAT ACTUALLY ENDS IT?`

segments.voice: The school is Samkhya. Tradition names the sage Kapila as its source, and it's usually read through a short book of verses, the Samkhya Karika. Its first verse says: because we are struck by three kinds of pain, we want to know what removes it. Commentators sort them as the hook did: pain from within, in body and mind; pain from other beings; and pain from forces beyond us. Then an objector speaks. Why bother with philosophy? There's medicine. It doesn't say medicine is bad. It says the seen remedies are not certain and not final. The pain returns. The second verse goes further: even the rituals of the Veda are like the seen remedies. They help, but they come with flaws and they wear off. Better, the verse says, is knowing three things: what is manifest, what is unmanifest, and the knower. That's where the counting comes in. Some take the name Samkhya to mean counting, others discernment; either way, the school goes through reality item by item. Its third verse sorts everything into a root that comes from nothing else, things that come from it and give rise to more, and things that only come from others. Add them up and you have twenty-four principles. And one more stands outside the count, neither made nor making anything. It comes tomorrow. Samkhya doesn't start with God or with atoms. It starts with pain, and an honest question about what really ends it.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF PAIN.` · `SEEN REMEDIES DON'T FINISH IT.` · `KNOW THE WORLD, AND THE KNOWER.` · `TWENTY-FOUR, AND ONE MORE.` · then, large: `IT STARTS WITH PAIN.`

segments.voice: Count ten breaths, starting again at one if you lose count. Then bring to mind one pain you're carrying and simply sort it, from within, from another person, or from the world, noticing that something in you can name it. If you pray, you can hold that pain before God. If it's ever too heavy, or you think of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Samkhya. A school that begins with three kinds of pain, looks for what truly ends it, and counts out the world, twenty-four principles and one more.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. The fixes in the drawer help, but don't finish the job. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and it is taught alongside Yoga, its paired school among the darshanas.

Index title/carry read 'Samkhya (the 24 principles' (closing parenthesis missing in the outline parse); kept exactly as the validator requires. The spoken carry says 'Samkhya, the twenty-four principles', matching day 1172.

'Twenty-four principles' is the sum of Karika 3's categories (1 root + 7 + 16), with purusha as the twenty-fifth; the verse itself gives 1, 7 and 16, not 24. Confirm the spoken phrasing 'add them up and you have twenty-four'.

Karika 1–2 paraphrased: duhkhatraya; seen means are aikanta/atyanta-less (not certain, not final); Vedic means are like the seen, with impurity, decay and excess; knowledge of vyakta, avyakta and jña is better. Confirm the gloss of the Vedic critique is fair and not framed as disrespect to the Veda.
The three kinds of pain (adhyatmika, adhibhautika, adhidaivika) as named by commentators (Gaudapada): confirm.
